web_title: 6. Multi-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Capital Structure
book_title: Chapter 6: The Forensic Ledger — 5-Year Financials, Cash & Dilution
question: Do Yash Highvoltage's 5-year P&L, balance sheet, cash conversion, return ratios, and equity raises hold up under forensic scrutiny?

epigraph.quote: Rapid revenue growth funded by equity is easy to admire; the forensic question is whether incremental capital earns its keep once the working-capital tide settles.
epigraph.author: Financial Forensics Principle

web_blocks.html: Between FY22 and FY26, Yash compounded revenue at ~38% CAGR, from ₹65.06 crore to ₹235.1 crore [1][10]. Over that same span, PAT compounded at ~44% CAGR from ₹8.71 crore to ₹37.4 crore [1][10]. Growth sped up in H1 FY27, with revenue up 95% YoY to ₹194.5 crore [1][3]. EBITDA surged 136% YoY to ₹54.7 crore (28.1% margin) [1][3]. PAT jumped 165% YoY to ₹36.2 crore (18.6% margin), nearly matching full-year FY26 PAT in six months [1][3].

web_blocks.caption: 5-Year Financial Forensics Summary (FY22–FY26 & H1 FY27, ₹ Crore)
web_blocks.takeaway: Gross margin expanded +800 bps from FY24 (40.3%) to H1 FY27 (48.3%) via RIP mix & operating leverage; H1 FY27 CFO surged to ₹45.2 Cr (125% of PAT) [1][10].

web_blocks.title: 6.2 Cash Conversion, Working Capital & Balance Sheet Forensics

web_blocks.html: A forensic cash-flow check explains the sole historical blemish in Yash's numbers. From FY22 to FY26, cumulative PAT totaled ~₹91.2 crore against ~₹44.7 crore of cumulative CFO, a ~49% conversion ratio [1][10]. Rapid growth absorbed working capital each year, peaking in FY26 when inventory jumped from ₹29.67 crore to ₹66.65 crore [1][10]. That build left FY26 CFO at ₹8.82 crore against ₹37.4 crore of PAT [1]. H1 FY27 broke that trend cleanly. Inventory rose just ₹5.1 crore to ₹71.8 crore on nearly doubled revenue [1]. Trade payables and customer advances grew, pushing CFO to ₹45.2 crore (125% of PAT) [1].

Total debt peaked at ₹31.09 crore in March 2026 (0.17x D/E) and fell to ₹10.30 crore by September 2026 (₹5.4 Cr long-term; ₹4.9 Cr short-term) [1]. With cash and deposits near ₹95.6 crore (net cash ₹95 crore), solvency risk is negligible [1][2]. Return ratios moderated after equity raises expanded net worth from ₹41.73 crore (Mar-24) to ₹319.60 crore (Sep-26) [1]. ROCE moved from 43.6% (FY23) to 25.1% (FY26), while ROE moved from 40.4% to 22.5% [1]. Meanwhile, ₹17.2 crore of CWIP and ₹10.3 crore of intangibles under development await Jarod's ramp [1].

web_blocks.title: 6.3 Share Dilution, Preferential Issue & Ownership Governance

web_blocks.html: Yash tapped equity markets twice in two years to fund expansion without debt. First, the December 2024 BSE SME IPO raised ~₹70.34 Cr for Jarod plus ₹14.76 Cr for GCP [1][10]. Second, the June 2026 ₹151 crore preferential issue funded Phase 2 550 kV core capacity [1]. That round paired equity shares with ₹60 Cr in warrants (25% upfront) backed by WhiteOak Capital, ValueQuest, Motilal Oswal, and Malabar India Fund [1][6]. On September 30, 2026, Promoters held 53.79% (50.57% fully diluted) with 0.0% pledge [6]. Mutual Funds held 2.45%, AIFs held 7.23%, and the Employee Benefit Trust held 3.36% [6].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Watchpoints Entering H2 FY27 & FY28
paragraphs: 1. Receivable Days: DSO rose from 47 days in FY26 to 66 days in H1 FY27 as receivables grew from ₹30.6 Cr to ₹69.5 Cr on Q2 billings [1][2]. Collection discipline must hold.
2. Post-Dilution Capital Efficiency: Equity now stands at ₹319.6 Cr with ₹114 Cr of capex left to deploy. Keeping ROCE above 22–25% requires hitting Jarod utilization and export targets.

web_blocks.title: 6.4 Quarterly & Half-Yearly Margin Progression Through H1 FY27

web_blocks.html: Half-yearly results across H1 FY26 → H2 FY26 → H1 FY27 show steady margin expansion, not a one-quarter spike [1]. Revenue climbed from ₹99.59 crore (H1 FY26) to ₹135.5 crore (H2 FY26) and ₹194.5 crore (H1 FY27), up 44% HoH and 95% YoY [1]. Over those three periods, gross margin rose from 42.4% → 45.9% → 48.3% [1]. EBITDA margin expanded from 23.3% → 27.4% → 28.1%, while PAT margin climbed from 13.7% → 17.5% → 18.6% [1].

Basic EPS followed the same upward path even on a larger share count [1]. It rose from ₹4.77 in H1 FY26 to ₹8.31 in H2 FY26 and ₹12.48 in H1 FY27 [1]. Finance costs stayed low at ₹2.4 crore in H1 FY27 (1.2% of revenue, down from 2.2% in H1 FY26) [1]. Short-term debt fell from ₹24.74 crore in March 2026 to ₹4.9 crore in September 2026 [1].

book_paragraphs: Numbers can tell two different stories depending on whether you stop at the income statement or walk down into the cash-flow and balance-sheet footnotes. On the income statement, Yash Highvoltage looks like a textbook industrial compounder: revenue nearly quadrupled from ₹65.06 crore in FY22 to ₹235.1 crore in FY26, and then hit ₹194.5 crore in the first half of FY27 alone. Even better, gross margins expanded by 800 basis points in two and a half years—from 40.3% in FY24 to 48.3% in H1 FY27—as RIP bushings and aftermarket retrofits took a larger share of the mix.

When we walk into the cash-flow statement, however, we immediately spot the historical tension: between FY22 and FY26, Yash generated ₹91.2 crore of cumulative net profit but only ₹44.7 crore of operating cash flow. Why? Because every time revenue surged, the company had to pre-buy imported RIP cores and build buffer inventory—most visibly in FY26, when inventory jumped from ₹29.7 crore to ₹66.7 crore and kept CFO at ₹8.82 crore.

That is why H1 FY27 is such an important forensic checkpoint. With revenue up 95% year-on-year, inventory barely budged from ₹66.7 crore to ₹71.8 crore, and operating cash flow exploded to ₹45.2 crore—more than 125% of net profit.

book_subsections.title: Balance Sheet Fortification and the Price of Equity Dilution
paragraphs: You also need to account for how Yash financed its expansion. Rather than loading up on debt like the ill-fated power equipment makers of 2012, Keyur Shah raised equity twice—first in the December 2024 SME IPO, and again in June 2026 via a ₹151 crore preferential issue of shares and warrants to institutional funds. As a result, shareholders' funds swelled from ₹41.7 crore in March 2024 to ₹319.6 crore by September 2026, while total debt fell to ₹10.3 crore against ₹95 crore of net cash.

The natural consequence of raising equity ahead of factory commissioning is that ROCE and ROE compressed from their pre-IPO peaks of 40%+ down to the 22–25% range. With promoters still holding 53.79% and zero shares pledged, governance alignment is clean—now the newly built Jarod plant must earn its keep on that larger equity base.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Pre-funding a ₹220 crore greenfield plant with equity rather than debt is conservative and smart—it eliminates solvency risk if the cycle ever pauses, even though it temporarily dilutes return on equity until the new lines hit full utilization.

book_subsections.title: The Half-Yearly Step-Up: Checking Earnings Quality
paragraphs: Whenever a manufacturing company reports a 165% jump in net profit, a forensic analyst immediately checks whether the surge came from other income, lower tax rates, or accounting tricks. Let us run that check on Yash's H1 FY27 numbers.

In H1 FY27, other income actually fell 45% year-on-year from ₹2.0 crore to ₹1.1 crore, while the effective tax rate held steady at roughly 24.4% (₹11.7 crore tax on ₹47.9 crore PBT). The entire profit expansion came from core operations: gross margins climbed from 42.4% to 48.3%, operating leverage compressed employee costs as a percentage of sales, and finance costs barely moved while short-term debt dropped from ₹24.7 crore to ₹4.9 crore.

Combine that clean P&L with ₹45.2 crore of operating cash flow and ₹95 crore of net cash on the balance sheet, and you have one of the cleanest forensic profiles in the Indian power-equipment space—with receivable days at 66 days as the sole working-capital metric to keep under surveillance.
